units.translation: placing a hair of a wild beast
For they are enemies to whom it befell to mourn with a lock of hair
seeing this shorn lock of mourning hair
consider, having placed a lock of hair at the cutting
having robbed Nisus of his immortal hair
to cry aloud, utter a sound
to cry aloud, utter a sound
Cry aloud, tell the much-wandering maiden
I have authority to proclaim the power of the road
For I cry aloud my own suffering
and about yourself you cry aloud a lawless strain
crying aloud to you, child, your father's voice
so as to draw a clot of blood in milk
and he mixed the dear milk with a clot of blood
vomiting the clots of blood which you drew off
with which can be compared what Plato said in Rep. 8 p. 553b: ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν ὠθεῖ ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ ἐν τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ φιλοτιμίαν [he thrusts headlong from the throne in his own soul the love of honor].
thus Pauw: χρόνοισι Μ [with times M]
θρόνον [throne] erroneously for θρόμβον [clot], which see.
so that as quickly as possible he might sit on his father's throne
the male throne being left desolate
while he remains on the throne of Zeus
from where would I get a throne in the upper air?
persuasive confidence sits on the dear throne of the mind
or he rises from the thrones because of his wife
who will cast him out, unseen, from his tyranny and thrones
shame to the fatherland and to the ancient thrones
and I shall find him on his father's thrones
he seats this prophet as fourth on the thrones
then I, a prophet, sit down on the thrones
O Justice, O thrones of the Erinyes
I would wish now to have thrones near you
and on thrones with a single scepter you accomplish every debt
he thrusts headlong from the throne in his own soul the love of honor
where θρώισκουσο [leaping] (and ἐξέθρωισκον [they leaped out] Pers. 457) M: see under θνήσκω [to die].
ἐκθορίζων καὶ σπερματίζων, γεννῶν [leaping out and sowing seed, begetting]. Aeschylus in Amymone (fr. 13).
and the one who mounts begets
leaping out and sowing seed, begetting. Aeschylus in Amymone
he endured to become the sacrificer of his daughter
which Triclinius explains as τῆς φθορᾶς αἱ πνοαί [the breaths of destruction]. More probably Hermann reads θυηλαί [sacrifices].
the toils and miseries of Thyestes
which Triclinius explains as περὶ θυσίας διατρίβεις [you busy yourself with sacrifices].
you perform sacred rites with hopes of good tidings
I approached the altar with sacrificing hand
lulling to sleep the fragrant flame that consumes incense
I made a song at the tomb like a Thyiad
